subject: history
title: Reform, Chartists and Suffragettes Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll trace the 19th- and 20th-century fight for the vote — from reform to Suffragettes.
meta_desc: GCSE History — Reform Acts, Chartists, Trade Unions and the Suffragettes.
final_note: You traced how reform acts, the Chartists, unions and the Suffragettes won the vote for working people and women.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The 1832 Great Reform Act gave the vote to about 1 in 5 adult men.

Working-class voters were still excluded. From 1838 the Chartists demanded six points including votes for all men. Their three petitions were rejected — but most demands came true later.

In 1834 the Tolpuddle Martyrs were transported to Australia for forming a farm workers' union.

By the 1860s unions were legal. The 1888 match girls' strike and the 1889 London dock strike showed unskilled workers' power. The Labour Party was founded in 1900.

The NUWSS Suffragists (from 1897) campaigned peacefully.

The WSPU Suffragettes (from 1903) under the Pankhursts smashed windows and went on hunger strike. Women over 30 won the vote in 1918. Equal franchise at 21 came in 1928.

mcqs.q: What did the 1832 Great Reform Act actually do?
options: The 1832 Reform Act gave the vote to all working men.
Chartism failed because Queen Victoria personally banned the movement.
The 1832 Reform Act allowed women to vote for the first time.
It abolished rotten boroughs, redistributed seats to industrial towns, and extended the vote to about 1 in 5 adult men — still far short of democracy.

mcqs.q: Why did Chartism fail in the short term?
options: Chartism failed because no one supported it.
The 1832 Reform Act allowed women to vote for the first time.
Chartism failed because Queen Victoria personally banned the movement.
Mass petitions were rejected by Parliament; the movement split between moral-force and physical-force wings; economic improvement after 1848 reduced support.

mcqs.q: What did the 1928 Equal Franchise Act do?
options: Chartism failed because Queen Victoria personally banned the movement.
The 1918 Representation of the People Act gave all women the vote.
The 1928 Act gave women in Britain the vote for the first time.
It gave women the vote on the same terms as men — all adults over 21 — completing the process begun in 1918, which had only enfranchised women over 30 with property.
